YouTube](http://img.shields.io/badge/youtube-nf--core-FF0000?labelColor=000000&logo=youtube)](https://www.youtube.com/c/nf-core) ## Introduction **nf-core/genephylo** is a bioinformatics pipeline that ... 1. Prepare a BLAST database: download one from NCBI, build one from your own sequences, or use an existing one ([`BLAST+`](https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)) 2. Search for homologs of each seed gene (`blastn` or `tblastn`) and retrieve their sequences ([`BLAST+`](https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)), removing duplicates ([`SeqKit`](https://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit/)) 3. Assign species from the NCBI taxonomy and rename sequences as `SPECIES|GENE|ACCESSION` ([`ETE 3`](http://etetoolkit.org/)) 4. Extract the coding sequence, keeping the longest ORF per sequence ([`TD2`](https://github.com/Markusjsommer/TD2)) 5. Initial alignment ([`MAFFT`](https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/software/)) and fast gene tree ([`FastTree`](http://www.microbesonline.org/fasttree/)) 6. Reconcile the gene tree with the species tree ([`Treerecs`](https://project.inria.fr/treerecs/)) and select the orthogroup of each seed gene 7. Final alignment of the orthogroup ([`MAFFT`](https://mafft.cbrc.jp/alignment/software/)), refined codon by codon ([`MACSE`](https://www.agap-ge2pop.org/macse/)) 8. Final maximum-likelihood tree ([`IQ-TREE`](http://www.iqtree.org/)) ## Usage > [!NOTE] > If you are new to Nextflow and nf-core, please refer to [this page](https://nf-co.re/docs/get_started/environment_setup/overview) on how to set-up Nextflow. Make sure to [test your setup](https://nf-co.re/docs/get_started/run-your-first-pipeline) with `-profile test` before running the workflow on actual data. First, prepare a samplesheet with one row per gene of interest: `samplesheet.csv`: ```csv id,fastafile TSTG1,TSTG1_nt.fasta TSTG2,TSTG2_nt.fasta ``` Each row represents one gene (not a sample). `id` is the gene name, used to name all output files. `fastafile` contains a single seed sequence for that gene: a nucleotide CDS with `--blast_type nt`, or a protein sequence with `--blast_type aa`. You also need a species tree in Newick format (`.nwk`) whose leaf names are species codes (first 3 letters of the genus + first 3 letters of the species, e.g. `HOMSAP` for _Homo sapiens_; for three-part names, 3 + 2 + 1 letters, e.g. `CANLUF` for _Canis lupus familiaris_). Now, you can run the pipeline using: ```bash nextflow run nf-core/genephylo \ -profile \ --input samplesheet.csv \ --blastdb_option build \ --blastdb_build sequences.fasta \ --blastdb_buildmap taxid_map.txt \ --species_tree species_tree.nwk \ --outdir ``` `--blastdb_option` selects how the BLAST database is provided: `build` (from your own sequences, as above), `update` (download a pre-formatted NCBI database, set with `--blastdb_update`) or `current` (an existing database, given with `--blastdb_dir`). > [!WARNING] > Please provide pipeline parameters via the CLI or Nextflow `-params-file` option. Custom config files including those provided by the `-c` Nextflow option can be used to provide any configuration _**except for parameters**_; see [docs](https://nf-co.re/docs/running/run-pipelines#using-parameter-files). For more details and further functionality, please refer to the [usage documentation](https://nf-co.re/genephylo/usage) and the [parameter documentation](https://nf-co.re/genephylo/parameters). ## Pipeline output To see the results of an example test run with a full size dataset refer to the [results](https://nf-co.re/genephylo/results) tab on the nf-core website pipeline page. For more details about the output files and reports, please refer to the [output documentation](https://nf-co.re/genephylo/output). ## Credits nf-core/genephylo was originally written by Lea Picard. For further information or help, don't hesitate to get in touch on the [Slack `#genephylo` channel](https://nfcore.slack.com/channels/genephylo) (you can join with [this invite](https://nf-co.re/join/slack)). ## Citations An extensive list of references for the tools used by the pipeline can be found in the [`CITATIONS.md`](CITATIONS.md) file.
